html:
The Ancestral Puebloans, once called the Anasazi, were the farming people of the Four Corners region of the southwestern United States, where Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and Colorado meet. The map shows them in 800 and 900.

Archaeologists divide their history into the Basketmaker period, when people lived in pit houses and wove fine baskets, and the Pueblo periods, when they built multi-storey houses of stone and adobe. They farmed maize, beans and squash in a dry land, and used round underground rooms, kivas, for ceremonies.

Their high points:

  • Chaco Canyon, with its great houses and long straight roads, from about 850 to 1150;
  • the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde, such as Cliff Palace, built in the 1200s.

In the late 1200s, during a long drought and times of conflict, they left the Four Corners and moved south and east. Their descendants are the Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples, who later led the Pueblo Revolt against Spain. The name Anasazi comes from the Navajo language, and many Pueblo people prefer "Ancestral Puebloans".
